transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, honestly, it was my work physical that got me here. The doctor there was going on about how my weight is too low. But I don't really get it, because to me I just feel... lighter on my feet, you know? Like for basketball. I play in this Tuesday night league with some of the guys, and man, I feel a lot quicker out there. 

Though last week, my buddy Dave—he works the parts counter with me—he completely blew out his knee on a rebound. Sounded like a wet branch snapping, it was awful. We had to wait like an hour for the ambulance because the dispatcher got the address mixed up with the elementary school down the road. 

But anyway, yeah, I just don't feel as weighed down at the garage anymore, either. Bending over those engine bays all day takes a toll. Especially the newer models, they pack everything in so tight you can barely fit a wrench down in there without taking off half the manifold. It's a real headache. But yeah, the work doc thought I should come see someone about the weight thing.
Do you think your weight is normal?

Normal? I mean... I know people are getting all worked up about it. The doc at work, some of the guys... but I figure they’re just making way too big a deal out of it, you know? I'm still showing up for my shifts, taking care of what needs doing around the house, still playing ball on the weekends. 

Actually, speaking of the house, I finally got around to fixing my riding mower this past weekend. The carburetor was completely gunked up. You leave that ethanol gas sitting in there over the winter, and it just turns straight to varnish, I swear. I had to soak the whole assembly in carb cleaner for like two days. My neighbor, Rick, he comes over while I'm working on it and tries to tell me I should just throw it out and buy one of those new electric ones. Electric! Can you believe that? For a half-acre lot with a steep grade... I told him, Rick, those lithium batteries die after three years and cost as much as a whole new mower anyway. It's a total scam, if you ask me. 

But anyway, yeah... I'm getting everything done just fine, so I really don't see what the big panic is about my size.
Do you think you are underweight?

Underweight? I mean, like I said, I know people are getting all worked up about it, but I figure they're just making way too much of it. I'm still showing up for work, taking care of the house, playing ball... I'm doing everything I normally do. 

Like yesterday, I was at the shop and we had this '08 Silverado come in. The guy was complaining about a rough idle and a check engine light. I pull the codes, right? P0300, random misfire. So I start checking the usual suspects—plugs, wires, coils. Turns out, it was a vacuum leak. The intake manifold gasket was just completely shot. I had to pull the whole top end off. Took me about four hours, but I got it running like a top again. The customer was thrilled, tipped me twenty bucks. You don't see that much anymore, people tipping mechanics. Usually they just complain about the bill, like I'm the one setting the prices for OEM parts. It's ridiculous how much a simple sensor costs these days. 

But yeah, I'm working just as hard as I ever did, so I really don't think I'm underweight or anything to worry about.
Do you think you look too thin?

Too thin? Look, honestly... I look in the mirror and I just don't see it. I know people are worried, like I said, but I really figure they're just making way too much of it. I mean, I'm still showing up for work every day, I take care of everything that needs doing at home, I'm playing ball on the weekends... 

Speaking of ball, we actually have a tournament coming up next month. It's this charity thing they do every year over at the community center. Last year, the gym floor was an absolute disaster. I don't know who they hired to refinish it, but they must have used the cheapest polyurethane on the market because it was like playing on an ice rink. Guys were slipping everywhere. My buddy Mike—he plays point guard for us—he slid right into the bleachers and sprained his wrist. Had to wear a brace for three weeks, couldn't even hold a wrench properly at his job. He does plumbing, mostly commercial stuff. Which, man, talk about a rough gig. He was telling me about this job they did at a restaurant downtown where the grease trap backed up into the main line. Said the smell was so bad they had to wear respirators just to get down in the basement. 

But anyway, yeah, I'm staying active, getting all my work done, so I really don't think I look too thin or anything like that.
Do you feel like you're eating enough?

Eating enough? I mean, yeah, I do what works for me. Most days I just keep it to coffee in the morning, and then maybe a small sandwich or half of whatever's around later on. Between the shop always running late and keeping up with the house, I just feel better sticking to my own simple rules, you know? Keeps things efficient. 

Actually, speaking of the shop running late... man, we had this absolute nightmare job yesterday that kept me there past seven. Guy brings in a 2015 F-150, says the brakes are making a "slight squeak." A squeak! I pull the wheels off and the rotors are completely gouged. Just metal on metal. The calipers were practically grinding into dust. I ask him when he last had the pads checked and he looks at me like I'm speaking Russian. It just blows my mind how people ignore basic maintenance. It's not rocket science. 

It's exactly like my brother-in-law, Dave. He bought this gorgeous Bayliner boat a couple years back. Takes it out on the lake all summer, but refuses to properly winterize the outboard motor. I keep telling him, Dave, that block is going to crack the second we get a hard freeze here. You can't just throw a cheap blue tarp over it and call it a day. But try telling him anything, right? He always knows best. He actually tried to wire his own hot tub last spring and kept tripping the main breaker for the whole street. 

But anyway, yeah... I stick to my simple rules with my meals and I get everything done just fine.
Are you afraid of gaining weight?

Afraid? Well... I guess you could say that. I mean, if I see the scale bump up even a pound, or if my work jeans feel tighter, I just start thinking I’m getting soft, you know? Like I’ll be slower moving around cars at the shop, or up and down the court on weekends. You gotta stay quick and agile in my line of work. Especially when you're dealing with low clearances. 

Actually, just this past Tuesday we had this '98 Corvette in the bay. Beautiful car, torch red, but man, the ground clearance on those things is a joke to begin with, and this guy had lowered it even more. Put these aftermarket coilovers on it. I don't get why guys do that to a daily driver around here. Every speed bump becomes Mount Everest, you know? Anyway, I was trying to get the low-profile jack under the front crossmember and I practically had to lay flat on my stomach just to see what I was doing. He was complaining about a scraping noise, and I look under there and his exhaust is basically dragging on the pavement. I had to weld a new hanger bracket on the mid-pipe. 

Took me way longer than it should have because my MIG welder was acting up again. The wire feed kept jamming every time I tried to lay a bead. I swear I need to just bite the bullet and buy a new Lincoln Electric setup, but the prices on equipment right now are absolutely through the roof. It's like everything else, I guess. Supply chain this, inflation that. 

But yeah, if I put on weight and get soft, I just wouldn't be able to maneuver around the shop or the court like I need to.
Do you think gaining weight would affect your performance in basketball?

Well, yeah, absolutely. Like I was saying, you gotta stay light on your feet. If I put on weight, I'd just feel sluggish out there. You lose that quick first step, and in our league, that's everything. 

Speaking of the league, though, I'm pretty sure we're going to have to find a new center this season. Big Dave—not my brother-in-law Dave, different Dave—he transferred to the night shift at the distribution center. He drives a forklift over at that massive Amazon warehouse they built off Route 9. You know the one? It's like a million square feet or something ridiculous. Anyway, he says the night shift pays a differential, which is great for him, but it completely screws up our practice schedule. 

And man, working nights really messes with your head. I did it for a few months back when I was just starting out, working at a 24-hour towing company. It was miserable. You're trying to sleep at noon, the sun is blazing, the neighbor is mowing his lawn... I actually ended up putting aluminum foil over my bedroom windows just to block out the light. My landlord threw an absolute fit about it. Said it looked like a crack house from the street. He was this grumpy old guy who used to measure the grass with a ruler to make sure the landscaping crew was cutting it exactly to two inches. 

But yeah, to answer your question, gaining weight would definitely slow me down on the court. I just can't afford to lose my edge out there.
Do you think gaining weight would change how you see yourself?

Change how I see myself? I don't know, I haven't really thought about it like that. I guess I just see myself as a guy who gets the job done, you know? Keep things tight, keep things running. 

Speaking of keeping things running, I finally got around to fixing the lawnmower this weekend. It’s this old Toro push mower I’ve had for probably fifteen years. Briggs & Stratton engine. The thing is an absolute tank, but the carburetor was completely gummed up. I knew I should have drained the gas at the end of last season, but I got lazy. Anyway, I’m out there in the driveway on Sunday with carburetor cleaner spraying everywhere, and my neighbor, Phil, comes wandering over. 

Phil is one of those guys who always has to one-up you, right? Like, if you caught a five-pound bass, he caught a ten-pounder. So he starts telling me about this new electric riding mower he just bought. Zero-turn, dual battery packs, the whole nine yards. Says it’s completely silent and he can mow his half-acre in twenty minutes. I’m just looking at him, holding a wrench, thinking, "Phil, you have a perfectly flat, square yard. You don't need a zero-turn mower." Plus, what happens when those lithium batteries die in three years? A replacement pack is probably half the cost of the mower. 

I tried explaining to him that there's something satisfying about fixing a simple gas engine yourself. You clean the jets, check the spark plug, give the cord a pull, and when it fires up, you actually feel like you accomplished something. But he just smiled that smug little smile of his and went back to his perfectly manicured lawn. I swear, the guy uses a weed whacker like he's performing surgery. 

But yeah, I don't know if gaining weight would change how I see myself. I just focus on staying sharp for work and the games.
Do you think gaining weight would make you feel less in control of your life?

Control? Well... I don't really look at it like that. I mean, I'm not really sure. Things are either working right or they aren't, you know? 

Speaking of things being out of control, though, you should have seen this 2014 Subaru Outback that got towed into the shop yesterday afternoon. Talk about losing control—the power steering pump was completely shot. The lady said it started making this high-pitched whining noise a week ago, which, you know, is classic power steering fluid cavitation. But she just kept driving it anyway until the rack and pinion seals blew out completely. ATF fluid everywhere. I'm not kidding, it looked like a crime scene under the hood. 

And trying to get parts right now is just a total nightmare. I called my guy over at NAPA, Jimmy. Good guy, known him for years, usually gets me whatever I need in an hour. But he tells me the steering rack for that specific year is on backorder. So I have to call around, and I finally find a remanufactured one at a warehouse two towns over. They send their new delivery driver—this kid who looks like he literally just got his learner's permit. He pulls up in this beat-up Chevy Colorado, music absolutely blasting, and proceeds to drop the box right in a puddle of antifreeze in our parking lot. I mean, the core charge alone on that rack is like eighty bucks, and this kid is treating it like a sack of potatoes. 

I had to spend half the afternoon just spraying down the Subaru's undercarriage with brake cleaner before I could even start wrenching on it. And brake cleaner is getting expensive, too. We go through cases of that stuff a week, and the shop owner is starting to complain about the overhead. 

But anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, right, the weight thing. Yeah, I don't really know about feeling less in control or whatever. I just try to keep myself running right so I can do my job.
Are you intentionally restricting your food intake to avoid gaining weight?

Well, I don't know if I'd call it restricting, exactly. It's more like... I just have my routine. Most days I keep it to coffee in the morning, and then maybe a small sandwich or just half of whatever is around later on. With the shop always running late and the house being so busy, I just feel better sticking to my own simple rules, you know? 

Speaking of coffee, though, you wouldn't believe what the new lube tech did to our coffee maker in the break room on Tuesday. We had this classic Bunn pour-over machine. The kind you see in old diners, right? Basically indestructible. Well, supposedly indestructible. This kid, Ryan, he decides the heating element isn't getting hot enough, so he tries to descale it using straight muriatic acid he brought from his garage. Said he read on some car forum that it cleans faster than white vinegar. I mean, it melted the internal plastic tubing completely. It smelled like a literal chemical fire in the shop for two days. We had to keep the bay doors open even though it was freezing out. 

So now we're stuck with this cheap single-serve pod machine the service manager bought at Walmart. The pods are ridiculously expensive, and half the time the puncture needle gets clogged with old grounds. I had to take a paperclip to it three times just this week to clear it out. I keep telling the guys we should just pitch in for a decent drip machine, but getting five mechanics to agree on spending twenty bucks each is like pulling teeth. My buddy Mike actually started bringing in his own vintage green Stanley thermos just to avoid dealing with the whole mess. 

But anyway, yeah. I just stick to my coffee and my simple rules. It just makes getting through the day easier.
Do you worry about gaining weight?

Worry about it? Yeah, I guess I do. If I see the scale bump up even a pound, or if my jeans feel just a little tighter, I start thinking I'm getting soft. Like I won't be able to move around the cars as fast, or I'll be slower up and down the court on the weekends. 

Speaking of moving around cars, though, I had the worst time getting under this lifted F-250 yesterday. The guy who owns it, he’s one of those guys who puts a six-inch suspension lift and thirty-five-inch mud tires on a truck that never leaves the pavement. You know the type. Spotless paint, chrome everywhere, not a scratch on the bed liner. Anyway, he brings it in because he’s got a vibration at highway speeds. I’m trying to check the U-joints on the driveshaft, and even with the lift, getting my creeper positioned right was a nightmare because of this massive aftermarket skid plate he had bolted on. 

And the creeper I use, it’s this old Snap-on one I bought off a retiring mechanic like ten years ago. It’s got these great polyurethane wheels that usually glide right over the rough concrete in our bays. But lately, the bearings in the front left caster have been grinding. Every time I shift my weight, it makes this awful screeching sound, like metal on metal. I keep meaning to order a replacement caster, but every time I sit down at the computer to do it, the phone rings or someone needs me to look at a diagnostic code. 

So I’m fighting with this creeper, trying to get leverage on the driveshaft of this giant truck, and the owner is standing right outside the bay door, just watching me. I hate when customers do that. It’s like, let me do my job, right? 

But yeah, the weight thing... I just don't want to get soft and slow down, you know? Gotta keep moving.
Do you think gaining weight would change how you feel about your appearance?

Change how I feel about how I look? Um... I don't know. I haven't really thought about it like that. I guess I just want to look like I can handle the work. You know, strong enough to get the job done. 

Speaking of getting the job done, we had this absolute nightmare of a job come in this morning. A 2008 Ford F-150 with the 5.4 Triton V8. If you know anything about those engines, you know exactly what I'm talking about—the spark plugs. It's a notorious design flaw. The plugs are a two-piece design, and carbon builds up around the shield. So when you go to back them out, they just snap right in half inside the cylinder head. 

I told the service manager, I said, "Look, quote the guy for the extraction tool labor right off the bat, because at least three of these are going to break." And sure enough, cylinder number four and cylinder number eight—the hardest ones to reach, right up against the firewall—they snap. So now I'm leaning over the fender of this truck, practically standing on my head, trying to use the Lisle extractor tool. You have to thread this pusher piece into the broken plug shell, press the porcelain down, and then thread a puller in to yank the rest of the sleeve out. It's nerve-wracking because if you mess it up, you're pulling the whole cylinder head off, which is easily a twenty-hour job. 

And my back is just killing me lately when I have to lean over engine bays like that. I used to use this thick foam fender cover to lean on, but someone borrowed it last week and never put it back. Probably that new kid, Ryan. The one who ruined the coffee maker. He leaves his tools everywhere, too. I tripped over a half-inch drive breaker bar he left right in the walkway between bays two and three yesterday. I swear, I spend half my day just managing the chaos in that shop instead of actually turning wrenches.

But anyway, yeah, my appearance... I just don't really think about it too much. I just need to look like I can keep working.
Do you think gaining weight would make you feel less attractive?

Less attractive? I mean... I don't really know. I don't really think about being "attractive." I'm a forty-four-year-old mechanic, you know? I'm usually covered in oil and brake dust by nine in the morning. I guess I just don't want to look out of shape. 

Speaking of looks, though, you should see this 1970 Chevelle SS we have sitting in the back lot right now. The guy brought it in for a rear main seal leak, but the paint job on this thing is just unbelievable. It's this deep cherry red, flawless clear coat. But the funny thing is, the owner is absolutely paranoid about us scratching it. He literally made our service writer walk around the car with him for twenty minutes with a flashlight, documenting every microscopic swirl mark before he'd even hand over the keys. 

And I get it, you know, it's a beautiful classic. But we're a mechanical shop, not a high-end detailing studio. My buddy Stan, who usually handles the heavy engine work, he actually refused to take the ticket because he didn't want the liability. Stan's got these massive hands and he's always dropping things. Just last month he dropped a three-eighths ratchet right onto the fender of a Honda Accord and left a dent the size of a golf ball. We had to call in our Paintless Dent Repair guy, Jimmy, to come massage it out from the inside so the customer wouldn't notice. Jimmy is an absolute wizard with those little metal rods, I swear. He just works the metal from behind the panel and it pops right back into place like it never happened. Charges an arm and a leg, though, and he only takes cash. 

So anyway, I ended up doing the rear main seal on the Chevelle myself. I just had to wrap the fenders in double layers of moving blankets before I even leaned over the bay. 

But yeah... what were we talking about? Attractiveness? I don't know. I just don't really focus on that kind of stuff for myself.
Do you think gaining weight would make you feel less attractive to others?

Attractive to others? Uh... I don't really think so. I'm not exactly out there trying to impress anybody these days, you know? I mean, my ex-wife used to joke that I cared more about transmissions than people anyway. I just don't have the energy to worry about what other people think of how I look. 

Speaking of trying to impress people, though, we had this kid come into the shop yesterday. He was maybe nineteen, twenty? Brought in this clapped-out 2012 Nissan Altima. You know the ones with those CVT transmissions that just grenade themselves right around eighty thousand miles? Anyway, he brought in this cheap, bolt-on aftermarket exhaust system he bought off the internet. Said he wanted it to sound aggressive because he was taking his new girlfriend out this weekend. I tried to tell him, I said, "Kid, it's a four-cylinder Altima, it's just gonna sound like a weed wacker trapped in a tin can." But he wouldn't listen. 

So I put it up on the two-post lift—the one in the far right bay where the hydraulic pump has been whining for a month. We really need to get the fluid flushed on that lift, but the owner is too cheap to call the maintenance guys out. Anyway, I'm under this Altima, and the rust on the exhaust flanges is just unbelievable. Northeast winters, man, the road salt just eats the undercarriage alive. I had to get the oxy-acetylene torch out just to heat up the bolts cherry red so they wouldn't snap off in my hands. The whole time, this kid is pacing around the waiting room, looking through the glass, probably texting that girlfriend about his sweet new ride. Took me two hours just to get the old rusted pipe off because the mid-pipe practically disintegrated when I touched it. 

But yeah... worrying about being attractive to others? It's just not really on my radar. I just want to stay light on my feet so I can get through the workday.
Do you think gaining weight would make you feel less confident about yourself?

Confident? I mean, yeah, I guess it hits my confidence. Like, if I see the scale bump up even a pound, or if my work jeans feel even a little bit tighter, I immediately start thinking I’m getting soft. I worry that I’ll be slower moving around the cars, or slower up and down the court. 

I play in this Thursday night pickup basketball league over at the community center. Just a bunch of older guys, you know, trying not to pull a hamstring. My buddy Dave from the parts department plays on my team. Dave is a big guy, probably pushing two-eighty, and he just camps out under the rim. He can barely jump anymore. He jokes that his shocks and struts are completely blown out. 

Speaking of Dave, he's the one who orders our parts at the shop, and lately, getting anything in on time has been a total joke. Like last week, we had this 2015 Jeep Grand Cherokee come in for a heater core replacement. If you've never done a heater core on one of those newer Jeeps, it is a massive headache. You literally have to pull the entire dashboard out of the vehicle. The steering column, the center console, the infotainment screen, the airbags—all of it has to come out just to get to the HVAC box buried deep against the firewall. It looks like a grenade went off in the front seat when you're halfway through the job. 

So I get the whole thing torn apart, my back is killing me from contorting myself under the dash, and I go to the parts window. Turns out Dave ordered the heater core for the dual-zone climate control, and this Jeep was just a base model with the single-zone. The inlet pipes didn't even line up. So now I've got this customer's interior completely gutted, plastic trim pieces taking up half my bay, and we're stuck waiting three days for the dealership to send the right part. I had to put all the screws and retaining clips in these little labeled Ziploc bags just so I wouldn't lose my mind trying to put it all back together days later. The customer was calling the service desk twice a day screaming at us, like it was my fault. 

But anyway... what was I saying? Oh, right, getting soft. Yeah, I just need to stay light so I don't slow down. I can't afford to be slow when I'm working or playing.
Do you think gaining weight would make you feel like you're losing control over things?

Losing control? I mean, no, not really. I don't look at it like that. It's not like my whole life is spinning out or anything just because of a few pounds. I just... I don't know, I just don't want to be heavy. 

Speaking of losing control, though, you should have seen this 2018 Ford F-250 that got towed into the shop on Tuesday. The guy said he completely lost control of the truck on the interstate. He was white as a ghost when the tow driver dropped him off. Turns out, his outer tie rod end had completely sheared off right at the steering knuckle while he was doing seventy in the left lane. 

He's incredibly lucky he didn't roll the thing into the median. You get those big heavy-duty trucks, especially the three-quarter tons with the solid front axles, and if the steering components get even a little bit of play in them, you can get what we call the "death wobble." The whole front end just starts shaking so violently the steering wheel practically gets ripped out of your hands. I got it up on the heavy alignment rack—the big drive-on one we usually reserve for the commercial box trucks—and the whole front suspension was just completely shot. Ball joints, track bar, drag link, all of it just chewed to pieces. The guy had put these massive thirty-five-inch mud tires on it but didn't upgrade the steering stabilizer to handle the extra rotational mass. 

I had to spend half my Wednesday just pressing out the old rusted ball joints with a heavy-duty C-clamp press. My shoulders are still burning today from cranking on that breaker bar trying to pop them loose. We had to order all new heavy-duty Moog parts just to put it back together so it was actually safe for the road. 

But anyway... what were you asking? About my weight and control? Yeah, I don't really think about it like a control thing. I just try to keep the numbers down on the scale, that's all.
Do you believe that gaining weight would significantly affect how you perceive yourself?

Perceive myself? Uh... no, not really. I mean, I'm just a mechanic. Gaining weight wouldn't change who I am fundamentally, you know? I'd still just be me. 

Speaking of perceiving things, though... it's funny you use that word, because we actually deal with that a lot at the shop now with all these newer cars. They literally have to perceive the road. Have you seen these newer Subarus? Like the 2020 Outbacks with that EyeSight system? 

We had one in on Monday. Guy caught a rock on the highway, cracked the windshield right down the middle. Used to be, you just swap the glass, run a bead of urethane, glue it in, and send them on their way in an hour. But now? Because of those dual cameras mounted up by the rearview mirror, when you put new glass in, the slight difference in the thickness distorts how the car perceives the lines on the road. You have to do this massive recalibration process. 

I spent three hours just setting up these giant black-and-white target boards in the bay. You have to measure the exact distance from the center of the hubcaps with a laser level, plumb bob it to the floor, and make sure the lighting in the shop is perfectly even. If there's a shadow on the board, or a glare from the open bay door, the camera fails the calibration and you have to start all over. And the whole time, our service writer is breathing down my neck because the customer is in the lobby throwing a fit about the labor charge. They just don't get that the car's computer basically needs a new prescription for glasses to see straight, otherwise the automatic braking will slam on the brakes for a shadow on the highway. 

But, uh... what were we talking about? Oh, me perceiving myself. Yeah, no, it wouldn't change my identity or anything like that. I just prefer to keep the weight off, that's all.
Do you believe that gaining weight would make you feel less like yourself?

Less like myself? Nah, not really. I mean, I'd still be me. It wouldn't change who I am on the inside or anything. I just... I really don't want to carry around the extra weight, you know? 

But it's funny you phrase it like that, because people actually say that about their cars all the time. They bring them into the shop and tell the service writer, "It just doesn't feel like itself lately." 

Like, we had this guy last month with a 2014 Chevy Silverado. It had the 5.3-liter V8 in it. He came in complaining that his truck felt like it had lost half its guts. Said it didn't sound right, didn't feel like his truck anymore. 

Sure enough, it was the AFM lifters. That's the Active Fuel Management system GM puts in those engines to shut down cylinders on the highway for better gas mileage. Honestly, it's a terrible design. The locking pins in the lifters get sludged up with oil and they collapse. So suddenly your big V8 is permanently running on four cylinders, and it sounds like a giant sewing machine ticking away under the hood. 

To fix it, you can't just pop a new lifter in. You have to pull the intake manifold, unbolt the exhaust manifolds, and take the entire cylinder head right off the engine block. And usually, by the time they bring it in, the bad lifter has already chewed a massive groove into the camshaft lobe. So then you're pulling the radiator, the water pump, the timing cover, all just to slide a new camshaft out the front of the engine. It turns into a thirty-hour job. The customer is looking at a bill for four grand just to make their truck feel like itself again. 

I spent three straight days covered in oil and coolant on that one job, busting my knuckles on the exhaust manifold bolts because they always snap off flush with the cylinder head on those LS engines. When that happens, you have to get the MIG welder out and weld a nut onto the broken stud just to back it out. It's a nightmare. 

But, uh... sorry, I completely lost track there. What was the question? Oh, right, me gaining weight. Yeah, no, I'd still feel like myself. I just really don't want the numbers on the scale to go up, that's all.
Do you avoid eating certain foods because you think they will make you gain weight?

Avoid eating certain foods? I mean, I guess. I just try to keep things pretty simple. Most days I just stick to coffee in the morning, and then maybe a small sandwich or just half of whatever happens to be around later in the day. With the shop always running late and things being so busy at the house, I just feel better sticking to my own simple rules, you know? It keeps things manageable.

Speaking of rules and keeping things simple, though, I wish these car manufacturers would stick to some basic rules when they design these engine bays. You should see what they did to the newer Ford Escapes. The battery placement is an absolute joke. 

I had a lady come in on Friday, just needed a new battery. The old one wouldn't hold a charge, dead cell. Used to be a five-minute job. Two ten-millimeter bolts on the terminals, maybe a bracket over the top, lift it out, drop the new one in. But on these Escapes? They shoved the battery so far back under the windshield cowl that you can't even see the negative terminal. You have to take off the wiper arms, pull off the entire plastic cowl assembly, unbolt the brake fluid reservoir, and remove the air intake tube just to get enough clearance to slide the battery out. 

It turned a five-minute job into an hour-and-a-half headache. And the customer is sitting there looking at me like I'm trying to rip her off on labor for a simple battery swap. I had to physically walk her out into the bay and show her how the engineers buried the thing. I swear, the guys designing these cars have never turned a wrench a day in their lives. They just design it on a computer screen and say, "Yeah, it fits," without thinking about the poor guy who has to service it five years down the road. 

But anyway... what were you asking? Oh, food. Yeah, I just stick to my coffee and half a sandwich. It's just easier that way.
Do you choose what you eat because you're afraid of gaining weight?

Choose what I eat because of that? I mean, yeah, I guess that's the main reason. If I see the scale bump up even a single pound, or if my work jeans feel tighter, I start thinking I'm getting soft. And I really can't have that. I worry that I'll be slower moving around cars in the bay, or slower up and down the court when I play hoops. 

Speaking of getting soft, though... you know what really gets soft? The air suspension on those older Lincoln Navigators. We had one in on Wednesday. Guy comes in complaining that the truck feels like a boat, just wallowing all over the road when he hits a bump. Sure enough, the rear air springs were completely shot. The whole rear end sags down to the bump stops, and the ride gets incredibly soft and bouncy. 

The dealership will charge you three grand to replace the compressor and the bags. But I always tell my customers to just do a coil spring conversion. You rip out all the air stuff and just bolt in standard steel coil springs and regular shocks. It rides a little stiffer, but it never fails on you again. The only annoying part is you have to wire a resistor into the suspension control module, otherwise the computer thinks the system is broken and flashes a "Check Air Ride" message on the dash every five seconds. I spent an hour crammed under the dash on Wednesday trying to find the right wire to splice into because the wiring diagram in our computer system was for the wrong year. My back was killing me after that.

Anyway, uh... sorry, I'm doing it again. What did you ask me? Oh, right, my food. Yeah, I just watch what I eat because I don't want to get soft and slow down. That's pretty much it.

So now I've got this customer's interior completely gutted, plastic trim pieces taking up half my bay, and we're stuck waiting three days for the dealership to send the right part. I had to put all the screws and retaining clips in these little labeled Ziploc bags just so I wouldn't lose my mind trying to put it all back together days later. The customer was calling the service desk twice a day screaming at us, like it was my fault. 

But anyway... what was I saying? Oh, right, getting soft. Yeah, I just need to stay light so I don't slow down. I can't afford to be slow when I'm working or playing.

doctor.intent: determine if patient has fear of gaining weight due to perceived loss of control
doctor.question: Do you think gaining weight would make you feel like you're losing control over things?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if gaining weight causes a feeling of losing control, which is a specific psychological aspect not covered by the patient's symptom profile (the closest symptom, Fear of Weight Gain, focuses on getting soft and slow, which was already addressed).

patient.answer:
Losing control? I mean, no, not really. I don't look at it like that. It's not like my whole life is spinning out or anything just because of a few pounds. I just... I don't know, I just don't want to be heavy. 

Speaking of losing control, though, you should have seen this 2018 Ford F-250 that got towed into the shop on Tuesday. The guy said he completely lost control of the truck on the interstate. He was white as a ghost when the tow driver dropped him off. Turns out, his outer tie rod end had completely sheared off right at the steering knuckle while he was doing seventy in the left lane. 

He's incredibly lucky he didn't roll the thing into the median. You get those big heavy-duty trucks, especially the three-quarter tons with the solid front axles, and if the steering components get even a little bit of play in them, you can get what we call the "death wobble." The whole front end just starts shaking so violently the steering wheel practically gets ripped out of your hands. I got it up on the heavy alignment rack—the big drive-on one we usually reserve for the commercial box trucks—and the whole front suspension was just completely shot. Ball joints, track bar, drag link, all of it just chewed to pieces. The guy had put these massive thirty-five-inch mud tires on it but didn't upgrade the steering stabilizer to handle the extra rotational mass. 

I had to spend half my Wednesday just pressing out the old rusted ball joints with a heavy-duty C-clamp press. My shoulders are still burning today from cranking on that breaker bar trying to pop them loose. We had to order all new heavy-duty Moog parts just to put it back together so it was actually safe for the road. 

But anyway... what were you asking? About my weight and control? Yeah, I don't really think about it like a control thing. I just try to keep the numbers down on the scale, that's all.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a fear of gaining weight due to its impact on their self-perception and body image
doctor.question: Do you believe that gaining weight would significantly affect how you perceive yourself?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether body weight or shape unduly influences self-evaluation, which is a symptom of Anorexia Nervosa but is not included in my specific symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Perceive myself? Uh... no, not really. I mean, I'm just a mechanic. Gaining weight wouldn't change who I am fundamentally, you know? I'd still just be me. 

Speaking of perceiving things, though... it's funny you use that word, because we actually deal with that a lot at the shop now with all these newer cars. They literally have to perceive the road. Have you seen these newer Subarus? Like the 2020 Outbacks with that EyeSight system? 

We had one in on Monday. Guy caught a rock on the highway, cracked the windshield right down the middle. Used to be, you just swap the glass, run a bead of urethane, glue it in, and send them on their way in an hour. But now? Because of those dual cameras mounted up by the rearview mirror, when you put new glass in, the slight difference in the thickness distorts how the car perceives the lines on the road. You have to do this massive recalibration process. 

I spent three hours just setting up these giant black-and-white target boards in the bay. You have to measure the exact distance from the center of the hubcaps with a laser level, plumb bob it to the floor, and make sure the lighting in the shop is perfectly even. If there's a shadow on the board, or a glare from the open bay door, the camera fails the calibration and you have to start all over. And the whole time, our service writer is breathing down my neck because the customer is in the lobby throwing a fit about the labor charge. They just don't get that the car's computer basically needs a new prescription for glasses to see straight, otherwise the automatic braking will slam on the brakes for a shadow on the highway. 

But, uh... what were we talking about? Oh, me perceiving myself. Yeah, no, it wouldn't change my identity or anything like that. I just prefer to keep the weight off, that's all.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a fear of gaining weight due to its impact on their self-perception and body image
doctor.question: Do you believe that gaining weight would make you feel less like yourself?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the influence of body weight on self-evaluation and identity (Criterion C of Anorexia Nervosa), which is not explicitly covered by the symptoms in the provided profile.

patient.answer:
Less like myself? Nah, not really. I mean, I'd still be me. It wouldn't change who I am on the inside or anything. I just... I really don't want to carry around the extra weight, you know? 

But it's funny you phrase it like that, because people actually say that about their cars all the time. They bring them into the shop and tell the service writer, "It just doesn't feel like itself lately." 

Like, we had this guy last month with a 2014 Chevy Silverado. It had the 5.3-liter V8 in it. He came in complaining that his truck felt like it had lost half its guts. Said it didn't sound right, didn't feel like his truck anymore. 

Sure enough, it was the AFM lifters. That's the Active Fuel Management system GM puts in those engines to shut down cylinders on the highway for better gas mileage. Honestly, it's a terrible design. The locking pins in the lifters get sludged up with oil and they collapse. So suddenly your big V8 is permanently running on four cylinders, and it sounds like a giant sewing machine ticking away under the hood. 

To fix it, you can't just pop a new lifter in. You have to pull the intake manifold, unbolt the exhaust manifolds, and take the entire cylinder head right off the engine block. And usually, by the time they bring it in, the bad lifter has already chewed a massive groove into the camshaft lobe. So then you're pulling the radiator, the water pump, the timing cover, all just to slide a new camshaft out the front of the engine. It turns into a thirty-hour job. The customer is looking at a bill for four grand just to make their truck feel like itself again. 

I spent three straight days covered in oil and coolant on that one job, busting my knuckles on the exhaust manifold bolts because they always snap off flush with the cylinder head on those LS engines. When that happens, you have to get the MIG welder out and weld a nut onto the broken stud just to back it out. It's a nightmare. 

But, uh... sorry, I completely lost track there. What was the question? Oh, right, me gaining weight. Yeah, no, I'd still feel like myself. I just really don't want the numbers on the scale to go up, that's all.

doctor.question: Do you avoid eating certain foods because you think they will make you gain weight?

target_item.name: Restrictive_Intake

target_item.reason: The doctor's question asks about avoiding certain foods to prevent weight gain, which is a direct inquiry into the restriction of food/energy intake.

patient.answer:
Avoid eating certain foods? I mean, I guess. I just try to keep things pretty simple. Most days I just stick to coffee in the morning, and then maybe a small sandwich or just half of whatever happens to be around later in the day. With the shop always running late and things being so busy at the house, I just feel better sticking to my own simple rules, you know? It keeps things manageable.

Speaking of rules and keeping things simple, though, I wish these car manufacturers would stick to some basic rules when they design these engine bays. You should see what they did to the newer Ford Escapes. The battery placement is an absolute joke. 

I had a lady come in on Friday, just needed a new battery. The old one wouldn't hold a charge, dead cell. Used to be a five-minute job. Two ten-millimeter bolts on the terminals, maybe a bracket over the top, lift it out, drop the new one in. But on these Escapes? They shoved the battery so far back under the windshield cowl that you can't even see the negative terminal. You have to take off the wiper arms, pull off the entire plastic cowl assembly, unbolt the brake fluid reservoir, and remove the air intake tube just to get enough clearance to slide the battery out. 

It turned a five-minute job into an hour-and-a-half headache. And the customer is sitting there looking at me like I'm trying to rip her off on labor for a simple battery swap. I had to physically walk her out into the bay and show her how the engineers buried the thing. I swear, the guys designing these cars have never turned a wrench a day in their lives. They just design it on a computer screen and say, "Yeah, it fits," without thinking about the poor guy who has to service it five years down the road. 

But anyway... what were you asking? Oh, food. Yeah, I just stick to my coffee and half a sandwich. It's just easier that way.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's eating habits are motivated by a fear of gaining weight
doctor.question: Do you choose what you eat because you're afraid of gaining weight?

target_item.name: Fear_of_Weight_Gain
target_item.manifestation: If I see the scale bump up even a pound or my jeans feel tighter, I start thinking I’m getting soft and that I’ll be slower moving around cars or up and down the court.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks if the patient's food choices are driven by a fear of gaining weight, which corresponds exactly to the 'Fear of Weight Gain' symptom.

patient.answer:
Choose what I eat because of that? I mean, yeah, I guess that's the main reason. If I see the scale bump up even a single pound, or if my work jeans feel tighter, I start thinking I'm getting soft. And I really can't have that. I worry that I'll be slower moving around cars in the bay, or slower up and down the court when I play hoops. 

Speaking of getting soft, though... you know what really gets soft? The air suspension on those older Lincoln Navigators. We had one in on Wednesday. Guy comes in complaining that the truck feels like a boat, just wallowing all over the road when he hits a bump. Sure enough, the rear air springs were completely shot. They dry rot over time, get these tiny hairline cracks, and the air just leaks right out. Then the air compressor runs constantly trying to keep the truck level until it just burns itself out and dies. The whole rear end sags down to the bump stops, and the ride gets incredibly soft and bouncy. 

The dealership will charge you three grand to replace the compressor and the bags. But I always tell my customers to just do a coil spring conversion. You rip out all the air stuff and just bolt in standard steel coil springs and regular shocks. It rides a little stiffer, but it never fails on you again. The only annoying part is you have to wire a resistor into the suspension control module, otherwise the computer thinks the system is broken and flashes a "Check Air Ride" message on the dash every five seconds. I spent an hour crammed under the dash on Wednesday trying to find the right wire to splice into because the wiring diagram in our computer system was for the wrong year. My back was killing me after that.

Anyway, uh... sorry, I'm doing it again. What did you ask me? Oh, right, my food. Yeah, I just watch what I eat because I don't want to get soft and slow down. That's pretty much it.
